newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-BRITISH HOPES FRUSTRATED AS PIOLINE ADVANCES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BRITISH HOPES FRUSTRATED AS PIOLINE ADVANCES.

text.p: British tennis was still awaiting its first Wimbledon men's semifinalist for 24 years after Greg Rusedski and the local weather each failed to rise to the occasion on Thursday.

Rusedski rarely hinted at the form which propelled him into the last eight as he lost 4-6 6-4 4-6 3-6 to France's Cedric Pioline in the first instalment of a British 'double bill' on the new Court Number One.

Tim Henman's bid to emulate Roger Taylor, the last British man to reach the semifinals in 1973, was then frustrated by rain after just six minutes of his quarter-final with former champion Michael Stich.
In that time, the 22-year-old Henman had already forced a break point but, at 0-1, 15-0, play was halted for the umpteenth time in the 111th championships and the covers were rolled back on.
Rusedski had no-one to blame but himself after his challenge petered out tamely on a cool, windy day.

His massive serve failed to dig him out of early trouble and Pioline, ranked 44th in the world, played with increasing assurance to become only the second French semifinalist at Wimbledon in the Open era.
"I felt I had a chance but Cedric was just too good today. He played awfully well.
"I'm just disappointed I couldn't play better for the crowd. It was a case of the mind saying 'I want to go down there and do my best' and the body saying 'No'."
The Canadian-born Rusedski, who has played 21 matches in the past three and a half weeks, did win the second set, spurred on by a fan urging him to 'do it for England'.

But an astonishing reflex forehand return from Pioline earned a vital early break in the third and the talented Frenchman, a finalist at the U.S. Open in 1993, could yet become the first Gallic winner since 1946.
"I don't like everything about Wimbledon, but I feel comfortable here," Pioline said. "The longer the match went on, the easier I was able to read his serve."

Rusedski is convinced he will have other chances in the future -- " I don't feel like I'm the full package yet" -- but the British crowds stood accused of not fully appreciating a notable day for their country's tennis.
Despite two contenders in the eight for the first time since 1961, there were numerous empty seats on Court Number One, even when Henman's match began.
"I was not that surprised as it was an 1100am start and the weather did not look particularly good," insisted Rusedski. "The crowd that was there was extremely vocal and very supportive."

Even so, the situation will raise further questions about Wimbledon's ticketing policy in the wake of People's Sunday, when the unavailability of pre-booked seats helped encourage a much more vibrant atmosphere.
